Push for the ratification of Maputo protocol

Through combined efforts by the WCW consortium and its coalition members, South Sudan approved the Maputo Protocol on June 7, 2023, in an unplanned but noteworthy success. Efforts at advocacy included visits to MPs to further the Protocol's acceptance and continuous commitment. After this historic mark, SIHA WROs are stepping up their efforts to guarantee the efficient execution of the Protocol, concentrating on budget allocation, guiding development plans, and actively supporting democratic processes, including elections.

comment.narrative: The Transitional Constitution and Bill of Rights (2011) provide guarantees for equality between women and men and a 25% affirmative action quota for women in legislative and executive bodies. The peace process increased this commitment to 35%. Also, there is incompatibility between the Constitution and customary law, which remains unaddressed and is a major barrier to the achievement of gender equality and the advancement of women’s rights. Push for 35% quota for women as was agreed upon during the peace process and address the incompatibility between the Constitution and customary law

The Transitional Constitution and Bill of Rights (2011) provide guarantees for equality between women and men and a 25% affirmative action quota for women in legislative and executive bodies. The peace process increased this commitment to 35%. Also, there is incompatibility between the Constitution and customary law, which remains unaddressed and is a major barrier to the achievement of gender equality and the advancement of women’s rights. Push for 35% quota for women as was agreed upon during the peace process and address the incompatibility between the Constitution and customary law

Although the 35% quota is not yet achieved, the WCW coalition in South Sudan has been involved in advocating for reform, particularly controversial parts on customary weddings and marital rape, which have delayed the adoption of the Family Law Bill. SIHA WROs in South Sudan have been aggressively fixing gaps in it. The WCW Coalition members are addressing these concerns using coordinated talks with the Ministry of Gender, Child, and Social Welfare (MOGCSW). With help from the WCW project, the Women for Justice and Equality group also obtained sub-grants to promote the Family Law bill and the anti-GBV legislation. Aiming to hone the measure to better address women's interests and rights, their efforts resulted in the anti-GBV bill being recalled from parliament for more talks with civil society organizations and women's groups.
In 2021, the project focused on establishing 3 coalitions (Juba, Wau, and Bentiu) and strengthening their capacity to advocate for law and legal reforms.
In 2021, the focus will be on mapping and identifying WRAs and Os to participate in the project, establishing coalitions, and engaging in capacity-building activities for the WRAs and Os.

Over the following two years, constant lobbying and awareness-raising campaigns will go toward teaching women's groups and citizens about their rights under these laws and the means of efficient application.

WRO/As in South Sudan have made strong progress in shaping laws and policies to advance women’s voice, agency, and leadership. In 2024, they influenced 6 key legal frameworks and policies, including the Anti-GBV Bill, Family Law Bill, Child Protection Law, and Transitional Justice Mechanism Bill,

comment.narrative: The baseline quantitative values are zero at this point as this indicator defines an increase. In South Sudan, WROs operate in one of the most challenging environments in the world. Stateservices are unable to provide basic education, health care or livelihood supports, andinfrastructure remains weak. Subsequently, initial gains in the formation of a national gendermachinery have not translated into women’s leaders, rights or agendas being equally included instate structures or policies. The space for civil society in South Sudan is limited and marred withlegal and regulatory obstacles that prevent WROs and the women’s movements from thriving. Thelegal restrictions, combined with the high risk of intimidation, imprisonment, and violence facedby activists, have limited the operational capacity of WROs and caused the flight of key championswithin the women’s rights movement. Prevailing media censorship environment also limits theextent WROs can engage the media as allies.

title.narrative: Number of women led CSOs with strengthened capacity to advance women’s rights and gender equality

description.narrative: Women-led organizations have strengthened capacity to advance women's rights and gender equality

comment.narrative: The baseline quantitative values are zero at this point as this indicator defines an increase. The baseline assessed the WROs capacity to promote women leadership. Regionally, 84% of the organizations are involved in activities or projects that promote women’s access to leadership positions; Uganda (21)22%, Somaliland and South Sudan Both at 17(18%), Sudan 12(13%), Ethiopia 10(10%) and Somali 4(4%). The involvement of the organizations in projects that promote women’s access to leadership positions was reported to be to a great extent by most representatives (75)88%. However, there are few organizations from Somaliland reported to promote access to women leadership. A number of organizations reported project beneficiaries that had taken up leadership positions as a result of current interventions; Regionally 60(71%), Somaliland 14(15%), South Sudan 16(17%), Sudan 7(7%), Uganda 20(21%), Ethiopia 8(8%), Somali 3(3%). In South Sudan, the social status of women is largely shaped by the impact of the 22-year civil warand entrenchment of customary laws10. Decision making in both private and public spheres isviewed as the role and responsibility of men with most women having little or no involvement indecision-making11 . Practices such as child marriage or arranged marriages lead to many girlsdropping out of school subsequently limiting women's chances of continuing education, which iskey to them pursuing careers in politics and other professions. Nonetheless, the return of manyqualified women to South Sudan following independence and the important role that womenshould play in the political, economic and cultural development cannot be underestimated.WROs in South Sudan occupy a unique niche with respect to playing key roles in peace building, nation building, promoting women’s public voice and participation in multiple layers of governance, and in linkingwomen and girls to services. WROs have gained some strategic experience in pushing forwardgender change agendas during long periods of historical conflict and displacement. They lobbiedfor the affirmative action quota and have been key to localizing UNSCR 1325. WROs also trainwomen as politicians and peacemakers and take on the broad task of raising women’s and girls’awareness of their human rights. Membership based WROs provides opportunity for peer-to-peersupport, reinforces friendship and social bonds across ethnic groups. WROs are able to implicatechange makers and committed volunteers from the grassroots to the national levels. They arerelatively well linked into exogenous networks such as those associated with the humanitariancluster coordination system and regional women’s rights networks.WROs suffer key challenges in accessing funding due lack of organizational systems and structures,short term funding which in the most cases are humanitarian in nature, lack of fundraising skillsand limited ability to network and connect with prospective donors. Another notable impedimentis the stiff competition with other already well-established and networked national andinternational organizations. Further, most of the WRO operate at lower levels of the society hencelack visibility to attract funds. Other challenges include: limited access to the internet and othersocial media coupled with poor connectivity and high cost of internet where it does exist and HRcapacity challenges.
Out of the 56 respondents surveyed in 2024 to assess progress towards the indicator, these were the women who identified their initiatives as women-led.

Summary of Baseline findings: Most of the activists are freelance and engage on issues supported by various organizations. Current leadership status among the participants varied across the countries; Regionally 55(50%), South Sudan 13(93%), Sudan 17(68%), Somaliland 4(57%), Uganda 16 (34%), Somali 2(20%) and Ethiopia 3(38%). Most of these leadership positions are held at the community level. Additionally, at WROs level, the average number of female staff across the countries is 167.5 while that of the male is staff is 23.3. Several women have risen to leadership positions across the surveyed countries. Somaliland had the highest number of women in leadership positions at 34%. This was followed by Ethiopia with 32%. The remaining countries, South Sudan, Sudan Uganda and Somali, had a mean of less than 10% The perception of participants in political affairs was also assessed. Although not very positive across the region except for Uganda, almost half of the participants 39(35%) perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants; Uganda 27(57.4%), Ethiopia 7(87.5%) while only Somali 1(10%), South Sudan 1(7.1%), and Sudan 1(4.0%) and Somaliland 2(8.6%). Structural conditions limiting women’s participation in decision-making roles include high levels of illiteracy; low levels of education, awareness of women’s rights, and self-esteem; lack of energy/time outside of economic activities; and high rates of VAW/G. Some women face more barriers than others: women from minority clans; internally displaced women and other migrants living in camps and informal urban settlements; poor rural pastoral women; women with disabilities; young women.

comment.narrative: The baseline quantitative values are zero at this point as this indicator defines an increase. The attitude and practices towards women’s voice, agency, leadership and representative participation in decision-making processes is not low compared to other countries Since South Sudan has managed to get many women elected to leadership positions with the exception of the process being fair for women. 12/14 reported to have ever participated in political campaigns; 6/14 reported to to have run for political office; 8/14 reported they are interested in political affairs, 11/14 reported having knowledge on both electoral and governance process and only 1/14 perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants
The total WRAs/Os targeted over year 1,2 and 3 were 87

From the midterm review conducted in June 2023, out of the 87 WRAs supported by the project under the South Sudan Women’s Coalition, 38(44%) reported having held a leadership position, for example as a CEO, Director, Manager, or Chair of an association, group, political party, or other organization. In addition to assuming leadership positions, a large number of women engaged in platforms for decision-making. For example, the initiative assisted activists in interacting with the 'Gender is My Agenda' (GIMAC) conference, which convened South Sudanese grassroots women, women leaders, and groups that promote women's rights. Moreover, assistance was given to advocates for women's rights so they could attend the Africa Family Law Conference. South Sudanese WRAs were informed of a UNDP task team that was working on drafting the country's Family Law bill after this regional conference. To represent their coalition and have an impact on the bill's formulation, they aggressively pursued participation in the task group

Direct groups targeted will be women’s rights organisations and activists in Juba, Wau and Bentiu,who will be the beneficiaries of training, joint activities, small grants, advocacy and gender forums.90 women’s rights activists who will be the beneficiaries of training, joint activities, small grants, advocacy and gender forums. Also women and young women from excluded or vulnerable groups such as urban poor women,women with disabilities will be beneficiaries of extensive training, and supported in communityoutreach and advocacy activities, and advocacy and gender forums. We will work in Juba, Central Equatoria; Wau, Western Bahr el Ghazal; and Bentiu, Unity State. The selection of these locations ensures coverage of each of the three administrative regions of South Sudan, but also provides the opportunity to work with women and youth from numerous ethniccommunities.
In 2021, the focus will be on mapping and identifying WRAs and Os to participate in the project, establishing coalitions, and engaging in capacity-building activities for the WRAs and Os.
